Nobody told me about THIS bit. 🎷

“Payments on account.” Two words that have ruined more Januarys than the weather.

If your self assessment bill is over £1,000, HMRC usually asks for two advance payments towards next year’s tax as well: one by 31 January and one by 31 July. First year self-employed? That January bill can be nearly one and a half times what you expected.

Put a little aside every month from now and January becomes just another month.

Seven pension pots. Not ideal. 🙃

Around 3.3 million UK pension pots are lost or forgotten. If you’ve changed jobs a few times, one of them could easily be yours.

Where to start:
🔍 Dig out old payslips or P60s for employer names
🔍 Use the government’s free Pension Tracing Service to find scheme contact details
🔍 Contact each provider and ask for a current value
🔍 Get advice before combining anything. Some old pensions have valuable guarantees.

Tell me: how many jobs have you had? I’ll start. 👇

Employed you: pension paid in every month without lifting a finger.
Self-employed you: pension paid in by… nobody. 🫠

With auto-enrolment, you and your employer pay in at least 8% between you. Go self-employed and that simply stops, unless you start it yourself.

The good news? You get to choose how much, when, and where. Many self-employed people pay in a percentage of each good month rather than a fixed amount.

Which side are you on right now? Left or right? 👇

The full new state pension is £241.30 a week for 2026/27. But only if you’ve got 35 qualifying years of National Insurance. 👀

If you’ve been self-employed, had time out for children, or lived abroad, there may be gaps you don’t know about. Each qualifying year adds about £6.89 a week, for life.

Three things to do this week:
1️⃣ Check your state pension forecast on GOV.UK (search “check state pension”)
2️⃣ Look at your National Insurance record for missing years
3️⃣ Ask before you pay to fill a gap. It isn’t always worth it.

Only 4% of solely self-employed people save into a pension. Four. In a hundred. 🫠

When you were employed, your pension happened quietly in the background. The day you went self-employed, nobody paid in for you, and most people never restart it.

It isn’t because you’re bad with money. Your income goes up and down, and bills come first. Totally fair.

But a basic-rate taxpayer who pays £80 into a personal pension gets it topped up to £100 with tax relief. That’s free money most self-employed people leave on the table.

Me finding out HMRC now wants to hear from me four times a year 😅

Making Tax Digital started on 6 April 2026. If you're a sole trader or landlord with £50,000+ of income in 2024/25 (before expenses), you now keep digital records and send HMRC a quarterly update.

Not there yet? It drops to £30,000 in April 2027 and £20,000 in April 2028.

The next update is due 7 November. And breathe: a quarterly update isn't a tax return, and no tax is paid when you send it. Your return and bill are still due by 31 January.

My office: partly claimable. My colleague: sadly not 🐶

If you're a sole trader working from home, HMRC's flat rate means you don't have to measure your gas bill:
25–50 hours a month: £10
51–100 hours: £18
101+ hours: £26

Or claim a fair share of your actual costs, which can be worth more if you're home most of the week. Business phone and internet are claimed separately.

Your grooming tunic or protective clothing counts as a business expense. The jeans you happen to groom in don't, even when they're 50% fur by 10am. Clippers, shampoo, towels and your business insurance are all claimable too.
